title: Check yourself: collection capacity and resizing

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A deduplication step creates `new HashSet<>(3_500)` and then adds 3,500 distinct order ids to it, with the default load factor. What happens to the set's table during those adds?

options.text: It never doubles, since it has 3,500 buckets and doubles only past one element per bucket
options.says: the constructor rounds the bucket count up to a power of two, 4,096, and the table doubles above three-quarters of it, not above one element per bucket

options.text: It doubles at add 3,073, since it has 4,096 buckets and doubles past three-quarters of them
options.says: the int is a bucket count rounded up to a power of two, 4,096; the threshold is 4,096 x 0.75 = 3,072, so add 3,073 doubles it

options.text: It doubles at add 2,626, since it has 3,500 buckets and doubles past three-quarters of them
options.says: the bucket count is rounded up to a power of two first, 4,096, and the threshold is three-quarters of that

options.text: It never doubles, since it has 4,096 buckets and doubles only past one element per bucket
options.says: the table doubles when the size goes above capacity x load factor, 3,072 here, not when it goes above the bucket count

origin.section: A HashMap Is Sized in Buckets, and It Doubles at Three-Quarters Full

questions.stem: An hourly job puts 3,000,000 entries into `new HashMap<>()`, which resizes 18 times on the way. The team switches it to `HashMap.newHashMap(3_000_000)`. What changes most in what the job's callers see?

options.text: Total load time falls several-fold, since every skipped resize called hashCode() on each key again
options.says: HashMap stores each key's hash, so a resize doesn't call hashCode() again, and the moves over a whole load add up to fewer than two per entry

options.text: Total load time falls several-fold, since the puts between resizes each copied part of the table
options.says: the cost lands on the puts that cross the threshold; the moves over a whole load add up to fewer than two per entry, so the total can't fall several-fold

options.text: A few puts stop taking milliseconds, since each of those puts moved every entry into a new table
options.says: a resize moves every entry in the one put that crosses the threshold; pre-sizing removes those pauses more than it shortens the load

options.text: A few puts stop taking milliseconds, since each of those puts called hashCode() on every key for a new table
options.says: the pauses do go, but not for that reason: HashMap stores each key's hash and a resize never calls hashCode() again; the cost is moving every entry

origin.section: A Resize Moves Every Entry in One put

questions.stem: A shared cache is created as `new ConcurrentHashMap<>(300, 0.6f)`, starts with a table of 512 buckets, and receives 600 puts. At which put does it first double its table?

options.text: At put 308, since the 0.6 load factor stays the map's limit and 512 x 0.6 is 307.2
options.says: the load factor only decided the size of the first table; resizes after that come at three-quarters full

options.text: At put 384, since the map grows when its size reaches three-quarters of the 512 buckets
options.says: whatever load factor it was built with, a ConcurrentHashMap doubles when its size reaches 0.75 x capacity: 384 of 512

options.text: At put 385, since the map grows when its size goes above three-quarters of the 512 buckets
options.says: that is HashMap's rule; ConcurrentHashMap doubles when its size reaches the threshold, one put earlier

options.text: At put 513, since the 0.6 load factor only sized the first table and the map grows past its 512 buckets
options.says: the map doesn't wait until it holds more entries than buckets; it doubles when its size reaches three-quarters of them

origin.section: ConcurrentHashMap Is Sized in Entries, and Its Load Factor Only Sizes the First Table

questions.stem: A session registry is a `HashMap` that reached 400,000 sessions during a sale. By the next morning all but 1,000 have been removed, and new sessions keep arriving at a trickle. What is true of the map's table now, and after a call to clear()?

options.text: It has shrunk back by now, and clear() would leave its length as it is
options.says: remove() unlinks entries and leaves the table's length as it is; a HashMap never halves its table

options.text: It has shrunk back by now, and clear() would release the table
options.says: the table keeps its peak length through remove(), and clear() keeps it too

options.text: It still has its peak length now, and clear() would leave that length as it is
options.says: an emptied HashMap keeps its table through remove() and clear(); only replacing the map gives the memory back

options.text: It still has its peak length now, and clear() would release the table
options.says: clear() removes the entries and keeps the table

origin.section: An ArrayList Grows by Half When Full, and Nothing Shrinks on Its Own

concepts: A HashMap keeps the table it reached at its peak through remove() and clear(); only replacing the map gives the memory back.
A resize moves every entry in the one put that crosses the threshold, without calling hashCode() again, so pre-sizing removes a pause more than it speeds up the load.
